name: Displacement
description: The straight-line distance from start to finish, including direction

content.overview: Okay, here's a fun one: displacement is just about where you ended up compared to where you started. It doesn't care one bit about the wandering, twisty path you took to get there—only the straight line from A to B matters.
content.explanation:
So displacement is really answering one question: **how much did your position actually change?**

Displacement = final position − initial position.

And here's the important part—displacement is a VECTOR. That's a fancy way of saying it has both a size AND a direction. It's not enough to say "I moved 141 meters," you also need to say *which way*.

**Let's walk through it:**
Imagine you walk 100 meters north, then turn and walk 100 meters east.
- Distance = 200 meters (that's your feet doing the work—every step counts)
- Displacement = √(100² + 100²) ≈ 141 meters, pointing northeast (just the straight-line hop from where you started to where you're standing now)

**Here's one that'll click even faster:**
Say you walk 5 km away from home to grab groceries, then walk the same 5 km back.
- Distance = 10 km (your legs definitely felt all of it)
- Displacement = 0 km (you're literally back at your front door—no net change in position!)

Kind of wild, right? You did a bunch of walking, but as far as displacement is concerned, you went nowhere.

**So what's the real difference?**
- Distance is the total path length—just a number (scalar), no direction attached.
- Displacement is the direct change in position—magnitude AND direction (vector).

One more thing: displacement can absolutely be negative. Picture yourself moving 10 meters to the right, then 15 meters to the left—your displacement is -5 meters. The sign is just telling you which direction you ended up net.
keyPoints: It's a vector—magnitude AND direction, not just a number
Think of it as the straight-line shortcut from start to finish
It can be negative—the sign just tells you the direction
Distance is always ≥ the size of displacement
content.whyItMatters: Here's the thing—physics actually cares more about displacement than distance. Why? Because displacement tells you the real, net change in where something is, and that's exactly what drives velocity and acceleration. Master this one, and the next few topics get a lot easier.
